subtype: Boss expects excellence or expects nothing [Receiver]
passage: Sumit, you tell me your internship is just photocopies and you've stopped caring. Let your Mridul Chacha tell you about 1998. I was twenty, interning at an engineering firm in Nagpur, with another boy, Joy. On the first day the chief engineer read my college report and said, 'Good. I'll expect a lot from you.' From then on he gave me site drawings to check, real ones, and every Friday he sat with me and marked my mistakes in red. Some Fridays I went home embarrassed. By the end of three months I was catching errors the juniors missed. Joy got tea orders and filing. Nobody corrected him because nobody gave him anything to get wrong. By the second month he was reading the newspaper at his desk by eleven. He wasn't lazy, beta. He just had nothing to rise to. So go and ask for one real task. Then ask for the red pen.

qa.q: What did the chief engineer give Mridul Chacha to check?
qa.a: He gave him site drawings to check, real ones, and marked his mistakes in red every Friday.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel on some Fridays, and why did he keep going?
qa.a: Some Fridays he went home embarrassed by the red marks, but the honest feedback helped him improve until he caught errors the juniors missed.

qa.q: What does Chacha advise Sumit to do, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: He tells Sumit to ask for one real task and then for honest corrections, so Sumit can get the stretch and feedback that help an intern rise.

qa.q: How might Joy have seen those three months?
qa.a: Joy may have felt ignored and bored, with only tea orders and filing, so reading the newspaper by eleven made sense when nothing was expected of him.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, as an intern, a boss's high expectations brought him stretch work and honest feedback, while the other intern was treated as filler and coasted.

subtype: Boss expects excellence or expects nothing [Receiver]
passage: The week the monsoon flooded half of Chennai, only four people could reach the logistics startup's office, and two of them were interns. On Monday the manager, Revathi ma'am, handed Rukmini the phone. 'Rukmini, call the truckers and reroute the orders. You're good at this. I'll check your plan at four.' At four she went through it line by line: 'This part is sharp. This part will fail. Fix it.' Kamal, the other intern, was asked to update the attendance sheet. He finished it in ten minutes. Then he sat by the window watching the water rise in the street. Nobody asked him anything else. By Thursday Rukmini was talking to warehouse managers like she'd done it for years. Kamal had stopped offering to help. On Friday evening, alone at his desk, he opened a job site and started updating his CV. 'They don't need me here,' he told himself.

qa.q: What did Revathi ma'am ask Kamal to do?
qa.a: She asked him to update the attendance sheet.

qa.q: What was Kamal thinking by Friday evening?
qa.a: He was thinking 'They don't need me here', feeling useless and unwanted after a week of being given nothing real to do.

qa.q: At what point could Kamal have changed his week, and how?
qa.a: After finishing the sheet in ten minutes, Kamal could have asked Revathi ma'am for a real task, such as helping Rukmini with the reroutes, instead of waiting by the window.

qa.q: How might the week have felt for Rukmini?
qa.a: Rukmini was probably stretched and a bit nervous, but also proud, since the honest feedback at four each day helped her grow fast.

grounding: During a flood week, one intern whom the manager clearly expects much from gets hard work and honest notes and rises, while the other is given nothing and starts to give up.

subtype: Manager checks own expectations [Response]
passage:
Monday: Jeevan, twenty-six and newly made site supervisor, sat with the weekly plan for the housing project in Nashik. Slab inspection: Arvind. Structural checks: Arvind. Paperwork and material register: Rashmi. He frowned. Rashmi had the same degree and the same six months on site. Why had he done that? He couldn't find a reason, only a feeling.
Three weeks later: he rotated the plan. Rashmi got the third-floor slab inspection. She missed a crack near a column, and Jeevan walked her to it and explained, slowly, the way he always did with Arvind. She wrote it down and thanked him.
Two months later: at the review, Jeevan pulled out the inspection logs instead of trusting his impressions. Rashmi's were the most detailed on the site. Arvind's were good but rushed. Jeevan put both names on the next tower and wrote in his notebook: check the list, not the feeling.

qa.q: What did Rashmi miss during her first slab inspection?
qa.a: She missed a crack near a column.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel when he looked at the weekly plan on Monday?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, frowning when he saw he had given Arvind all the tough work for no reason but a feeling, though Rashmi had the same degree and experience.

qa.q: Which of Jeevan's choices made the plan fairer, and why?
qa.a: He rotated the tough tasks, gave Rashmi the same patient explanation he gave Arvind, and judged them later by their logs, not his impressions.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have seen the change in her work?
qa.a: Rashmi probably felt trusted and taken seriously for the first time, getting real inspections and patient feedback instead of only paperwork.

grounding: A young site supervisor notices he hands tough work to one engineer and routine work to another, then gives both the same challenge and patience and judges by the logs.

subtype: Manager checks own expectations [Response]
passage: Parul, you've just been made team lead and you're asking me how to be fair. Let old Vasudha tell you her mistake. At twenty-five I was made head of the primary section at a school in Indore, the youngest in the staffroom. That first year, I gave the science exhibition, the inspection lessons and the parents' meetings to Mrs Joshi, because she spoke well. Mrs Rao got the attendance and the timetable. In March I made the list for the annual report and saw it written down. I felt quite ashamed. I had never once watched Mrs Rao teach. So the next year, I made a rotation. Everyone got a big project, everyone got my notes, everyone got the same patience when things went wrong. And I looked at results, children's work, not at who sounded confident. Mrs Rao's class did the best model at the exhibition. Write your list down, Parul. The list doesn't lie.

qa.q: What did Mrs Rao's class do at the next exhibition?
qa.a: Mrs Rao's class did the best model at the exhibition.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel on seeing the list written down?
qa.a: Vasudha felt quite ashamed, seeing that one teacher had got everything big and the other only routine work, without ever being watched teaching.

qa.q: What changes did Vasudha make, and how can Parul use them?
qa.a: Vasudha rotated the big projects, gave everyone the same notes and patience, and judged by children's work; Parul can write down the team's task list and do the same.

qa.q: How might Mrs Rao have felt in that first year?
qa.a: Mrs Rao may have felt overlooked and underused, handling attendance and timetables while someone else got all the chances to shine.

grounding: A retired head tells a new lead how they once noticed giving the big tasks to one teacher and routine work to another, then gave all the same challenge and judged by results.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage: The overnight train to Kochi was packed and noisy, and Thomas, twenty-six, had his five-year-old son Chinmay tucked beside him on the lower berth. When the ticket checker smiled and asked, 'What's your name, little one?' Thomas answered, 'Chinmay. He's the shy one, he won't talk.' Chinmay pressed into his father's side. Across the aisle, three children were playing snap. 'Want to play?' a girl called. 'He doesn't like joining in,' Thomas said. Then his office phone rang, and it was his boss, and the connection kept dropping. He went to the door end of the coach to hear. It took twenty minutes. When he came back, Chinmay was sitting cross-legged in the middle of the other berth, slapping cards down. 'I'm Chinmay! I won two!' Thomas stood in the aisle holding his phone, suddenly unsure which of them had been shy.

qa.q: What did Thomas tell the ticket checker?
qa.a: Thomas said, 'Chinmay. He's the shy one, he won't talk.'

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he came back and saw Chinmay playing?
qa.a: He felt surprised and unsure, starting to wonder whether the 'shy one' label was really about Chinmay or about his own belief.

qa.q: What could Thomas try the next time someone asks Chinmay a question?
qa.a: He could wait and let Chinmay answer for himself, and let him decide whether to join games, instead of saying no for him.

qa.q: How might the girl who invited Chinmay see him now?
qa.a: She probably sees him as a fun, chatty player who likes winning at snap, not a shy child at all.

grounding: A young father sure his son is shy answers for him and turns down invitations, until a work call leaves the boy alone and he joins in by himself.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage: At the Diwali rangoli contest in their Gurugram apartment society, Sunaina held six-year-old Vikas's hand tightly. 'He's my shy one,' she told the organiser. 'He'll just watch.' The organiser offered Vikas a bowl of orange powder. Vikas looked at it for a long time. 'He doesn't like crowds,' Sunaina said, and gently moved the bowl away. At the snack table, when an aunty asked Vikas what class he was in, Sunaina said, 'First standard. He's quiet.' Vikas nodded. Later, his grandfather found him staring at the other children's patterns. 'Want to try, beta?' Vikas shook his head. 'I'm shy,' he said, very seriously. 'Mumma says.' Sunaina laughed and ruffled his hair. But that night, clearing up, she found a small orange handprint on the corner of the contest sheet, and nobody else's hand was that size.

qa.q: What did the organiser offer Vikas?
qa.a: The organiser offered Vikas a bowl of orange powder.

qa.q: What does the small orange handprint suggest about Vikas?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted to join in more than he showed, and that the 'shy' label may be holding him back rather than describing him.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do differently at the next event?
qa.a: She could let Vikas answer questions himself and let him take the bowl of powder if he wants, giving him room to try.

qa.q: How might Vikas's grandfather see what is happening?
qa.a: His grandfather may notice that Vikas repeats 'Mumma says' and worry that the boy is learning to be shy from what he hears.

grounding: A young mother sure her son is the shy one answers for him and keeps him from joining, and he starts repeating the label, though a small handprint hints he wanted to take part.

subtype: Small treat seems big or small by comparison [Actor]
passage: The train had been stuck outside Itarsi for three hours, and the only food left was a packet of plain glucose biscuits. Irawati, five, ate two without a word. Then Amma found one cream biscuit at the bottom of her bag. 'For you!' Irawati bounced on the berth, licking the cream slowly. Just then a lady opposite gave her brother Asif a big chocolate cookie. Irawati stopped licking. She looked at her little biscuit. Her lip shook. 'Mine is tiny,' she wailed.

qa.q: What was the only food left on the stuck train?
qa.a: The only food left was a packet of plain glucose biscuits.

qa.q: Why did Irawati's lip shake after Asif got the cookie?
qa.a: Next to the big chocolate cookie, her cream biscuit suddenly felt tiny and not special, so she felt sad.

qa.q: How could Amma help Irawati in that moment?
qa.a: Amma could hug her, remind her how happy the cream biscuit made her a minute ago, and maybe let Asif share a piece.

qa.q: How might Asif feel when Irawati wails?
qa.a: Asif might feel awkward or a bit guilty holding his big cookie while his little sister cries.

grounding: A five-year-old is thrilled with a cream biscuit after plain ones, then tearful when her brother gets a bigger cookie, showing how comparison changes a treat.

subtype: Small treat seems big or small by comparison [Actor]
passage: At the bakery near their Chennai flat, the baker gave Leela, five, a small star-shaped biscuit for free. Leela gasped and held it up to the light. 'A star! Seema Akka, look!' She did a little dance by the glass case. Then the baker handed her big sister Seema a large heart biscuit with pink icing. Leela stopped dancing. She looked at the heart, then at her star. 'Mine is small,' she whispered, eyes filling. Seema knelt. 'Your star was the best thing ever a minute ago.' Leela sniffed and looked at it again.

qa.a: It was a small star-shaped biscuit.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when she first got the star biscuit?
qa.a: She was delighted, gasping, holding it up to the light and doing a little dance by the glass case.

qa.a: The baker might feel sorry, since both biscuits were meant as a kind treat and one ended up making Leela sad.

subtype: Marks judged against friends [Actor]
passage: The school bus was stuck in a jam near the market, horns blaring, and Jagdish had forty minutes to stare at his English paper: 26 out of 40. He had been quite pleased when Ma'am handed it back. Then Preeti, beside him, showed hers: 38, with 'Excellent!' in green. Now his 26 looked terrible. His grandfather would ask about it at dinner. Jagdish folded the paper small and stuffed it in his bag. 'I'm hopeless,' he muttered. At the next stop, Preeti's mother climbed on, reading her phone. 'Ma'am has messaged the parents' group. The class average was only 21. Very hard paper, she says.' Jagdish sat up. He unfolded the paper. Twenty-six. Above average! By the time the bus reached his lane, he was grinning and practising how to tell Dadaji.

qa.q: What did Jagdish score in English?
qa.a: He scored 26 out of 40.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish mutter 'I'm hopeless'?
qa.a: Next to Preeti's 38 with 'Excellent!', his 26 suddenly felt terrible, and he worried about telling his grandfather.

qa.q: What could Jagdish ask himself next time he compares marks?
qa.a: He could ask what his mark means on its own, whether he improved or how hard the paper was, instead of judging it only against a friend's top score.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt seeing Jagdish fold his paper away?
qa.a: Preeti might have felt awkward that showing that mark made a friend upset, without meaning to.

grounding: A boy's same mark feels terrible next to a friend's top score and wonderful once he hears the class average, showing the reference point changed the feeling.

subtype: Marks judged against friends [Actor]
passage: In the Pune colony's evening tuition class, Chaitanya got his maths practice test back: 55 out of 100. He shrugged. Not bad. Then Lalit, at the next desk, waved his paper. '92! Beat that!' Chaitanya's ears went hot. Suddenly 55 looked like a failure. He slid the paper under his notebook and didn't answer the next question Sir asked. Then Sir tapped the board. 'This was an olympiad-level test. Most of you are between 30 and 45. The average is 38.' Chaitanya looked at his paper again. 55. Seventeen above average! He pulled it out and smoothed it flat. On the walk home through the colony, he swung his bag and told the watchman, the vegetable seller and his mother, in that order.

qa.q: What was the class average on the practice test?
qa.a: The average was 38.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya's ears go hot when Lalit waved his paper?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, because next to Lalit's 92 his 55 suddenly looked like a failure.

qa.q: Which question could help Chaitanya judge his mark more steadily?
qa.a: He could ask how hard the test was and how he did compared with his own past, rather than only comparing with Lalit's top mark.

qa.q: How might Lalit see Chaitanya after the average was announced?
qa.a: Lalit might notice his friend cheer up and realise that both of them did well on a very hard test.

grounding: A boy feels miserable about his fair mark after a friend's top score, then delighted when he hears the low class average, though his mark never changed.

subtype: Feeling plain after scrolling edited photos [Actor]
passage: In the girls' hostel study hall, free period, Payal scrolled for an hour with her book open underneath. Face after face: glowing skin, perfect brows, not a single mark. When she finally looked up, she caught her reflection in the dark window and winced. Her forehead was shiny. There was a spot on her chin. She pulled her hair forward and didn't go to evening games. Vandana, her roommate, dragged her anyway to the courtyard for badminton. Under the tube lights, everyone was sweaty and red-faced. Vandana had a rash from the heat. Somebody had a pimple on her nose and was laughing too hard to care. After twenty minutes Payal forgot to hide her chin. Walking back, she realised she hadn't thought about her face once. It was the same face. It had just stopped standing next to those photos.

qa.q: Where did Payal spend her free period scrolling?
qa.a: She scrolled for an hour in the girls' hostel study hall, with her book open underneath.

qa.q: How did Payal feel when she saw her reflection after scrolling?
qa.a: She felt plain and embarrassed, wincing at her shiny forehead and the spot on her chin, and wanted to hide.

qa.q: What choice helped Payal feel normal again, and why?
qa.a: Going to badminton with Vandana put her among real, sweaty, laughing classmates, so her face was no longer being compared with filtered photos.

qa.q: How might Vandana have seen Payal before and after badminton?
qa.a: Vandana probably saw her roommate hiding and low at first, and then relaxed and laughing once they were playing.

grounding: A teenage girl feels unattractive after an hour of polished photos, then feels normal among sweaty, laughing classmates, because the comparison set changed.

subtype: Feeling plain after scrolling edited photos [Actor]
passage:
Dear Salma Apa,
You said I could write to you about anything, so here's a weird one.
Last night I spent an hour on the photo app. Boys my age with perfect skin, sharp jaws, not one pimple. By the end I went to the mirror and my face looked wrong. My moustache is still that fuzzy dust thing. I have three spots on my forehead. I told Ammi I had a headache so I wouldn't have to go to the school trip today.
She made me go anyway. And Apa, on the bus, everyone looked like... people. Farooq has spots too. Manav has the same fuzzy moustache. Nobody's jaw was sharp. By the end of the day I'd forgotten my face existed.
Same face as last night. I checked. I think the app just made it stand next to the wrong faces.
Don't tell Ammi about the fake headache.
Your little brother,
Kiran

qa.q: What did Kiran tell Ammi to avoid the school trip?
qa.a: Kiran told Ammi he had a headache so he wouldn't have to go to the school trip.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after an hour on the photo app?
qa.a: He felt unattractive and uncomfortable, his face looking wrong in the mirror, enough to want to skip the trip.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Kiran saw his face?
qa.a: Going on the trip and seeing real classmates like Farooq and Manav with spots and fuzzy moustaches let Kiran see his face as normal again.

qa.q: How might Salma Apa respond to this letter?
qa.a: Salma Apa would probably feel protective and pleased that Kiran worked out the photos were the problem, not his face.

grounding: In a letter a teenage boy describes feeling plain after scrolling polished photos, then normal among classmates, noticing the comparison changed, not his face.

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage: At the crowded cloth shop in Meerut's main bazaar, Sachin, nineteen, needed something for his sister's wedding. His cousin Kashish had come along to keep him within budget: fifteen hundred rupees. The shopkeeper, smiling, first pulled out a velvet blazer with gold buttons. 'Fifteen thousand, sir. Pure quality.' Sachin laughed and shook his head. Then the man showed a printed silk shirt. 'Only three thousand.' 'Only three!' Sachin said. 'After that blazer this is almost free.' Kashish watched him reach for his wallet. Last week he had said a two-thousand shirt was 'robbery'. 'Sachin, what did you say about the two-thousand one?' He paused, hand on the wallet. 'That was different.' 'Different how? This one's more.' He looked at the blazer, then the shirt. 'Oh,' he said slowly. Kashish noticed he put his wallet back in his pocket, but his eyes kept going to the silk.

qa.q: How much was Sachin's budget for the shirt?
qa.a: His budget was fifteen hundred rupees.

qa.q: Why did Sachin say the silk shirt was 'almost free'?
qa.a: He had just seen the fifteen-thousand blazer, so three thousand felt tiny by comparison, even though it was double his budget.

qa.q: What did Kashish's question make Sachin notice, and what did he choose?
qa.a: Kashish reminded him he'd called a two-thousand shirt robbery, so he saw the price only looked cheap after the blazer and put his wallet back.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper see the blazer he showed first?
qa.a: The shopkeeper probably shows it on purpose, knowing it makes the next item look like a bargain to most customers.

grounding: A cousin watches a young man call a costly shirt cheap after being shown a very expensive blazer, and helps him notice that the comparison shaped the judgment.

subtype: Choosing the reference point deliberately [Response]
passage: Jomon, you're comparing your salary with your batchmates' posts again. Let your Seema Aunty tell you something. At twenty-five, I had just rented my first flat in Kozhikode, one room, a tiny kitchen, a window facing a wall. That same month, three friends posted photos of new homes: balconies, big sofas, one with a garden. I sat on my plastic chair and felt poor. Then I made myself ask three questions. What is this flat worth by itself? A safe door, my own kitchen, fifteen minutes from work. What was I living in two years ago? A hostel bed with four roommates. What do I actually need? Quiet to study and a stove. Answered like that, it was a good flat. Those photos were their best day, taken from the best angle. My plastic chair was my every day. So, beta, what does your salary do for you, compared with last year?

qa.q: What did Seema Aunty's first flat face?
qa.a: Its window faced a wall.

qa.q: How did Seema Aunty feel when she saw her friends' photos of new homes?
qa.a: She felt poor and discouraged sitting on her plastic chair, because she was comparing her everyday flat with their best-day photos.

qa.q: Which questions helped Seema Aunty, and how could Jomon use them?
qa.a: She asked what the flat was worth by itself, what she had two years ago and what she needed; Jomon could ask what the salary does for Jomon compared with last year.

qa.q: How might the friends who posted the photos have felt about their own posts?
qa.a: They were probably happy to share a good day, without knowing their best-angle photos were making someone else feel poor.

grounding: An aunt tells Jomon how she judged her first flat by its own worth, her own past and her needs rather than against friends' best-day photos.

subtype: Choosing the reference point deliberately [Response]
passage: The scooter showroom in Jaipur closed at eight, the festival discount ended tonight, and Yash, twenty-four, had until then to decide. The salesman had started with the top model: alloy wheels, digital screen, ninety-eight thousand. Next to it, the basic model at sixty-two thousand looked plain and cheap. His friend Tushar's new scooter was all over social media, with a sunset behind it. Yash's sister Aadhya checked her watch. 'Forty minutes.' Yash took a breath and wrote on the back of the brochure. What do I need? Ten kilometres to work, a helmet box, a bit of rain. What was I using before? A cycle and two buses. What is the basic one worth by itself? He read it back. 'The basic one does everything. It's a big step up from buses.' 'And the sunset photo?' Aadhya asked, grinning. 'Tushar's view, not my commute.' He signed for the basic model at 7:52.

qa.q: How far does Yash travel to work?
qa.a: Yash travels ten kilometres to work.

qa.q: Why did the basic scooter first look plain and cheap to Yash?
qa.a: He had just seen the top model with alloy wheels and a digital screen, and Tushar's sunset photos, so the basic one seemed small beside them.

qa.q: Which questions helped Yash choose under time pressure, and why did they work?
qa.a: He asked what he needed, what he used before and what the basic model was worth by itself, which moved the comparison away from the top model and Tushar's photos.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see her brother's choice?
qa.a: Aadhya seems pleased and amused, seeing him pick what fits his commute instead of chasing Tushar's view.

grounding: Under a deadline a young man judges a scooter by its own worth, his past and his needs, instead of against the costlier model and a friend's highlight photos.

subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
passage: At the amusement park near Kolkata, Trisha, fourteen, had four hundred rupees: enough for a snack and the giant wheel, which she'd been waiting all year to ride. At the popcorn stall, the board said: Small popcorn, ₹120. Medium popcorn, ₹230. Medium popcorn and juice combo, ₹240. 'Deepika, look. Ten rupees for a whole juice! That's basically free.' She had planned to get the small one. Instead she bought the combo, feeling very clever. Deepika bought the small. They ate on a bench. Trisha managed half the popcorn and a few sips of juice before she felt full. Then they reached the giant wheel queue. Tickets: ₹200. Trisha counted her money twice. One hundred and sixty. 'Wait, how?' Deepika looked at the half-eaten tub in her hand. Trisha stared at the wheel turning slowly above them.

qa.q: How much was the medium popcorn and juice combo?
qa.a: The combo was ₹240.

qa.q: Why did Trisha feel clever buying the combo?
qa.a: Next to the medium popcorn alone at ₹230, the juice seemed to cost only ten rupees, so the combo felt like a free bargain.

qa.q: At which point could Trisha have avoided losing the giant wheel ride, and how?
qa.a: At the stall, she could have compared the combo with the small popcorn she planned to buy and remembered she needed ₹200 for the ride.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel watching Trisha at the giant wheel queue?
qa.a: Deepika might feel sorry for a friend, and maybe think about offering to share or lend money for the ride.

grounding: A teenager picks a mid-size popcorn combo because a poorly priced medium popcorn makes it look like a bargain, then finds she can't afford the ride she wanted.

subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
passage:
'Movie night! Yamini, you're ordering snacks.'
'Okay, Mummy. Vaibhav, look at the menu. Small popcorn, ninety-nine. Medium popcorn, two-nineteen. Medium popcorn plus cold drink, two-twenty-nine.'
'Get the small. We have juice in the fridge.'
'Are you mad? The medium combo is ten rupees more than the medium. That's a free drink.'

'Genius,' he said.
'Shut up. I'll have it tomorrow.'

qa.a: It cost two-twenty-nine.

qa.q: How did Yamini feel when she ordered the combo?
qa.a: She felt smart with money and proud, calling it a free drink and 'Genius'.

qa.q: What question from Vaibhav could have changed Yamini's choice?

'Aditi, which data plan should I take? My phone plan ends tonight.'
'Show me, Zainab.'
'Plan one, one-ninety-nine, one GB a day. Plan two, four-forty-nine, one and a half GB. Plan three, four-seventy-nine, three GB a day plus a free video plan.'
'You use one GB a day, max.'
'But look at plan two! Thirty rupees less than plan three and half the data. Who takes plan two?'
'Nobody. That's the point.'
'What point?'
'Why would they make a plan nobody takes?'
'So I take plan three, obviously.'
'Or so you forget plan one exists.'
Zainab paused, thumb over the button. 'Plan one doesn't have the video thing.'
'Do you watch videos on your phone?'
'...Sometimes.'
'You watch on Abbu's TV.'
'Four-seventy-nine is still better value.'
Her big sister Aditi sighed. Zainab pressed plan three and felt clever for the whole evening.

qa.q: How much was plan three?
qa.a: Plan three was four-seventy-nine, with three GB a day plus a free video plan.

qa.q: Why was Zainab so sure plan three was 'obviously' right?
qa.a: Compared with plan two, which was only thirty rupees less for half the data, plan three looked like clear value, so she felt confident and clever.

qa.q: At which moment could Zainab have made a better choice, and how?
qa.a: When Aditi said she uses one GB a day at most, Zainab could have compared plan three with plan one and her real needs instead of with plan two.

qa.q: How does Aditi see the plan nobody takes?
qa.a: Aditi sees plan two as a trick to make plan three look good and to make people forget the cheaper plan that fits them.
